newsitem.title: USA: U.S. job growth resumes, moderate economy seen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. job growth resumes, moderate economy seen.

text.p: The U.S. economy created jobs at a healthy pace in October after jobs were lost in September, the government said Friday, while the unemployment rate was unchanged at 5.2 percent.
In the government's first look at the the economy last month, the Labour Department said the number of non-farm jobs rose by 210,000 after falling a revised 35,000 in September.

The report, which was nearly identical with Wall Street forecasts, seemed to show an economy that was forging ahead at a slower but sustainable pace with no indication that inflationary pressures were building.
It was reinforced by a smorgasbord of economic indicators from both government and private industry that pointed to slow but steady economic growth.

The reports were likely to be well-received at the Federal Reserve, the nation's central bank, which has held interest rates steady while waiting to see if the economy would slow from a brisk rate of growth last spring.
"You could hardly blame (Fed Chairman) Alan Greenspan now if he leaned out his office window and shouted 'Told ya so,'" said economist Bill Cheney of John Hancock Financial Services.

"It's a perfect number," said Evelina Tainer, chief economist at Indosuez Carr Futures. "The Fed's going to love it. It puts the three-month average at 152,000, which means we're growing at a nice pace but not too slow, not too fast."

The report came four days before the presidential elections and two days after the government said the economy slowed to a 2.2 percent rate of growth in the third quarter from a brisk 4.7 percent rate in the second quarter.

President Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole have each tried to put their own spin on the economic reports, with the president claiming his policies were fostering sustained expansion while Dole claimed a recession was in the making.

Katharine Abraham, Commissioner of the Bureau of Labour Statistics, noted that the unemployment rate has fallen from 7.3 percent in October 1992, before the last presidential election, and that payrolls have grown by 11.3 million.

The government said in a separate report that factory orders rose 2.7 percent in September after falling 2.1 percent in August. The Commerce Department said surging orders for aircraft offset weakness in most other product categories.
Two other reports by private groups pointed to moderating economic activity.

A survey of purchasing managers said manufacturing grew more slowly in October than in September. The National Association of Purchasing Management said its monthly index fell to 50.2 percent in October from 51.7 percent in September. A reading above 50 indicates growth in manufacturing, while one below that indicates contraction.

The Index of Leading Indicators, meant to forecast economic activity six to nine months ahead, rose in September for the eighth straight month, though it was the smallest of those increases, the Conference Board, a business research group said.
In its report, the Labour Department said average hourly earnings of workers, which have been widely watched recently as a possible sign of inflation, were unchanged.

The various reports will be closely eyed by Fed policy-makers at their next meeting on Nov. 13 to weigh their next move on interest rates. Most analysts expect the central bankers to leave rates unchanged and some are now saying the Fed may have to cut rates sometime early next year.
The department said service industries added 119,000 jobs, the largest gain since May, led by recreation businesses.
After little growth in August and September, the retail trade added 62,000 jobs in October.
Government employment fell another 40,000, while employment in both finance and real estate rose sharply.
Manufacturing employment rose 6,000 after falling in September.
